newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Talks on new Albania election law near deadline.
newsitem.headline: Talks on new Albania election law near deadline.

text.p: Albanian politicians were to resume negotiations over a new election law on Monday, but were running out of time as they searched for a compromise that would enable elections to go ahead next month, Western officials said.

The elections due on June 29 are a key part of the international drive to prevent Albania plunging once again into the violence that swept the country last March after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.

Under a political contract brokered by European envoy Franz Vranitzky and signed by the 10 main political parties, the law has to be approved today and passed by parliament this week to enable President Sali Berisha to announce the election day by May 15.
Under Albanian law, the president must call an election at least 45 days before voting takes place.
Berisha was set to hold a news conference on Monday at 0900 GMT, his first since the troubles began.

An official from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which is holding talks with politicians to thrash out details of the law, said more discussions would take place on Monday.
"We are very much concerned that it (the law) will be approved," the official told Reuters.
"It probably will be close, tactics are very important to get this common agreement," he added.
The main point of disagreement is over the number of seats that will be decided on a proportional basis and the number to be decided by a majority vote.
The dispute between Berisha's Democratic Party and the rest of the nine-party Government of National Reconciliation has threatened to scupper the planned elections.

The Democrats wanted most of the seats to be chosen by simple majority vote, as in the last elections in May 1996 when they won 122 of the 140 seats in parliament. But international observers said the election was flawed, and the opposition Socialists pulled out on the last day.
The rest of the government wants more seats to be chosen by proportional representation to allow the smaller parties a voice in parliament.
The OSCE official said the talks between politicians and election experts would be very techical. Each party was "making its point", he said.

The other main obstacle to the elections is the so-called Salvation Committees, groups which sprang up in several towns during the violence, mainly in the south of the country, to protect local citizens and restore some kind of order.

The political contract says the Committees must be disbanded no later than May 14, 46 days before the planned election. But the Committees say they plan to hold a meeting to decide their future only on May 16.
The Committees are strongly opposed to Berisha, blaming him for the collapse of the pyramid schemes and demanding that he quit.
Berisha in turn says the Committees are an armed wing of the opposition Socialists, though the Socialists deny they have any link with them.
